Student Activity 5: Mapping mixed customer profiles — solution

Instructor reference

Livio Finos, University of Padova

1 Scope of this reference

This is one defensible solution, not the only acceptable one. The data are synthetic, so the purpose is to make modelling decisions explicit: identifiers are not measurements, nominal labels have no numerical order, and variable importance is a choice to justify rather than a fact produced by software.

2 1. Data dictionary and distance specification

customers <- read_csv("data/customer_profiles.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    loyalty_tier = ordered(loyalty_tier, levels = c("Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum")),
    preferred_channel = factor(preferred_channel),
    region = factor(region),
    uses_discount = factor(uses_discount, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

dictionary <- tibble(
  variable = names(customers),
  type = c("identifier", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "ordinal",
           "nominal", "nominal", "binary symmetric", "numeric count"),
  include_in_distance = c("No", rep("Yes", 8)),
  reason = c(
    "Labels rows only; numerical differences between IDs are meaningless.",
    "Range-scaled numeric difference.", "Range-scaled numeric difference.",
    "Range-scaled behavioural frequency.", "Ordered ranks are meaningful.",
    "Only same/different is meaningful.", "Only same/different is meaningful.",
    "Both Yes and No are informative here.", "Range-scaled behavioural count."
  )
)
knitr::kable(dictionary, row.names = FALSE, caption = "One defensible variable classification.")
One defensible variable classification.
variable type include_in_distance reason
customer_id identifier No Labels rows only; numerical differences between IDs are meaningless.
age numeric Yes Range-scaled numeric difference.
income_k_eur numeric Yes Range-scaled numeric difference.
visits_last_month numeric Yes Range-scaled behavioural frequency.
loyalty_tier ordinal Yes Ordered ranks are meaningful.
preferred_channel nominal Yes Only same/different is meaningful.
region nominal Yes Only same/different is meaningful.
uses_discount binary symmetric Yes Both Yes and No are informative here.
returns_last_year numeric count Yes Range-scaled behavioural count.

The selected Gower dissimilarity is

\[d_G(i,j)= \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\,\delta_{ijk}\,d_{ijk}} {\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\,\delta_{ijk}}.\]

For numeric variables, \(d_{ijk}=|x_{ik}-x_{jk}|/R_k\), where \(R_k\) is the observed range. For nominal variables it is 0 for a match and 1 for a mismatch. For an ordered factor it is the scaled rank difference. In this baseline all weights are one; that is a transparent default, not proof that variables are equally important for every business purpose.

profiles <- customers |>
  select(age, income_k_eur, visits_last_month, loyalty_tier,
         preferred_channel, region, uses_discount, returns_last_year) |>
  as.data.frame()
rownames(profiles) <- customers$customer_id
d_gower <- daisy(profiles, metric = "gower")

pair_table <- function(d) {
  as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(d))) |>
    transmute(customer_1 = as.character(Var1), customer_2 = as.character(Var2),
              dissimilarity = Freq) |>
    filter(customer_1 < customer_2) |>
    arrange(dissimilarity)
}

pairs <- pair_table(d_gower)
pair_examples <- bind_rows(
  head(pairs, 3) |> mutate(comparison = "Closest"),
  tail(pairs, 3) |> mutate(comparison = "Most distant")
) |> select(comparison, customer_1, customer_2, dissimilarity)
knitr::kable(pair_examples, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Closest and most distant pairs for the equal-weight baseline.")
Closest and most distant pairs for the equal-weight baseline.
comparison customer_1 customer_2 dissimilarity
Closest C11 C24 0.012
Closest C04 C21 0.033
Closest C10 C20 0.058
Most distant C16 C22 0.902
Most distant C07 C24 0.913
Most distant C07 C16 0.934

Close pairs should share several characteristics, not necessarily every one. Conversely, a combination of different region, channel, discount use and loyalty tier can make a pair distant even when ages are similar.

3 2. MDS map and its limitation

fit <- cmdscale(d_gower, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
map <- customers |>
  transmute(customer_id, loyalty_tier, preferred_channel,
            MDS1 = fit$points[, 1], MDS2 = fit$points[, 2])

ggplot(map, aes(MDS1, MDS2, colour = loyalty_tier, shape = preferred_channel,
                label = customer_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(nudge_y = .025, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Customer profiles under equal-weight Gower dissimilarity",
       colour = "Loyalty tier", shape = "Preferred channel")

Classical MDS of the equal-weight Gower dissimilarities. The axes are arbitrary coordinate directions, not customer traits. 

map_distance <- dist(fit$points)
cor(as.vector(d_gower), as.vector(map_distance))
## [1] 0.9447721

The map gives a compact view of major profile contrasts. It is not complete: Gower dissimilarity is not guaranteed to be Euclidean, and two dimensions cannot preserve every pairwise distance. The correlation printed above is a descriptive diagnostic of distance reproduction, not an acceptance threshold.

4 3. Why arbitrary numeric codes are not valid

If Mobile = 1, Store = 2 and Web = 3, Euclidean distance says that Mobile is twice as far from Web as it is from Store. Replacing the codes with Mobile = 1, Store = 3 and Web = 2 reverses that geometry without changing the observed categories. The numerical gaps come from the coding decision, not the data. A nominal variable should enter through a same/different comparison.

5 4. Homework extension

5.1 4.1 Give recent visits double weight

weight_visits <- c(age = 1, income_k_eur = 1, visits_last_month = 2,
                   loyalty_tier = 1, preferred_channel = 1, region = 1,
                   uses_discount = 1, returns_last_year = 1)
d_weighted <- daisy(profiles, metric = "gower", weights = weight_visits)

knitr::kable(head(pair_table(d_weighted), 6), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Closest pairs after giving visits double weight.")
Closest pairs after giving visits double weight.
customer_1 customer_2 dissimilarity
C11 C24 0.011
C04 C21 0.038
C10 C20 0.051
C03 C13 0.087
C01 C02 0.092
C07 C08 0.095

The weighting is defensible only if visit frequency is genuinely twice as important for the stated segmentation purpose. It must be documented and checked as a sensitivity analysis; choosing weights merely because they create a desired visual grouping is not defensible.

5.2 4.2 Remove age and income

profiles_behavioural <- profiles |> select(-age, -income_k_eur)
d_behavioural <- daisy(profiles_behavioural, metric = "gower")
fit_behavioural <- cmdscale(d_behavioural, k = 2)

behavioural_map <- customers |>
  transmute(customer_id, loyalty_tier, preferred_channel,
            MDS1 = fit_behavioural[, 1], MDS2 = fit_behavioural[, 2])
ggplot(behavioural_map, aes(MDS1, MDS2, colour = loyalty_tier,
                            shape = preferred_channel, label = customer_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(nudge_y = .025, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Profiles after removing age and income",
       colour = "Loyalty tier", shape = "Preferred channel")

Removing age and income changes the target from demographic-plus-behavioural similarity to engagement and preference similarity.

Removing variables changes the scientific question; it is not merely a graphical adjustment. This version compares engagement, loyalty and preferences rather than a broader demographic-plus-behavioural profile.

5.3 4.3 Distance-reproduction plot

original <- as.matrix(d_gower)
mapped <- as.matrix(map_distance)
reproduction <- tibble(
  customer_1 = rownames(original)[row(original)[upper.tri(original)]],
  customer_2 = colnames(original)[col(original)[upper.tri(original)]],
  original_distance = original[upper.tri(original)],
  map_distance = mapped[upper.tri(mapped)]
) |> mutate(absolute_error = abs(original_distance - map_distance))

ggplot(reproduction, aes(original_distance, map_distance)) +
  geom_point(colour = blue, alpha = .7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = orange, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Original Gower dissimilarity versus map distance",
       x = "Gower dissimilarity", y = "Two-dimensional MDS distance")

Pairs far from the diagonal are poorly reproduced by the two-dimensional map. 

knitr::kable(slice_max(reproduction, absolute_error, n = 1),
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Pair with the largest distance-reproduction error.")
Pair with the largest distance-reproduction error.
customer_1 customer_2 original_distance map_distance absolute_error
C07 C15 0.264 0.042 0.222

The pair with the largest error deserves inspection, but it is not necessarily an error in the data. It is a relationship that cannot be retained faithfully in this two-dimensional representation.

6 5. Example decision memo

We compared anonymised customer profiles, excluding the identifier. We used Gower dissimilarity because the variables include numeric measures, an ordinal loyalty tier, nominal channel and region, and binary discount use. Numeric differences were scaled by observed ranges and baseline weights were one. Classical MDS gives an exploratory map in which nearby points have similar profiles under this explicit specification. The axes are not customer traits, and the map does not reproduce every dissimilarity exactly. Any weighting must be tied to a documented purpose. Customer profiling can also amplify unfair treatment or support inferences beyond the data, so the map is not an automated decision rule.
